title: Negative Results for Software Effort Estimation

edges.target: COCOMO-II model and 2000 tunings (Boehm et al.)
edges.ref: [7] Barry Boehm, Ellis Horowitz, Ray Madachy, ... Chris Abts. Software Cost Estimation with Cocomo II. Prentice Hall, 2000.
edges.evidence: we use COCOMO since its internal details have been fully published [7]. Also, we can access a full implementation of the 2000 COCOMO model.

edges.ref: [7] Boehm et al. Software Cost Estimation with Cocomo II. Prentice Hall, 2000.
edges.evidence: We consider data expressed in terms of the COCOMO ontology: 23 attributes describing a software project, as well as aspects of its personnel, platform and product features

edges.target: COC81 data (1981 COCOMO book), via PROMISE repository
edges.ref: [5] B. Boehm. Software Engineering Economics. Prentice Hall, 1981.
edges.evidence: COC81 is the original data from 1981 COCOMO book [5]. This comes from projects dating 1970 to 1980.

edges.ref: http://openscience.us/repo (no numbered reference; 'NASA data collected in the early 1990s')
edges.evidence: NASA93 is NASA data collected in the early 1990s about software that supported the planning activities for the International Space Station.

edges.ref: [50] Tim Menzies, D. Port, Z. Chen, J. Hihn, and S. Stukes. Validation methods for calibrating software effort models. In Proceedings, ICSE, 2005.
edges.evidence: Menzies' preferred local calibration procedure is the COCONUT procedure of Figure 6 (first written in 2002 and first published in 2005 [50]).

edges.ref: [8] L. Breiman, J. H. Friedman, R. A. Olshen, and C. J. Stone. Classification and Regression Trees. 1984.
edges.evidence: we also compare COCOMO-II and COCONUT with CART and Knear(n) as they proved their value in the 1990s [68, 73].

edges.ref: [68] M. Shepperd and C. Schofield. Estimating software project effort using analogies. IEEE TSE, 23(12), November 1997.
edges.evidence: Knear(n) estimates a new project's effort by a nearest neighbor method [68]. ... it is not always true the parametric estimation has been superseded by ... Knear(n)

edges.ref: [73] Fiona Walkerden and Ross Jeffery. An empirical study of analogy-based software effort estimation. Empirical Softw. Engg., 4(2):135-158, 1999.
edges.evidence: When estimating for n > 1 neighbors, we combine estimates via the triangle function of Walkerden and Jeffery [73]

edges.ref: [75] Peter A. Whigham, Caitlin A. Owen, and Stephen G. Macdonell. A baseline model for software effort estimation. ACM TOSEM, 24(3), May 2015.
edges.evidence: We also baseline the COCOMO-II and COCONUT models using the Automatically Transformed Linear Baseline Model(ATLM) proposed by Whigham et al. [75].

edges.ref: [34] E. Kocaguneli, T. Menzies, A. Bener, and J. Keung. Exploiting the essential assumptions of analogy-based effort estimation. IEEE TSE, 28:425-4...
edges.evidence: to account for some of the more recent work on effort estimation, we also use TEAK and PEEKING2 [34, 60]. ... nothing was ever ranked better than COCOMO-II or COCONUT.

edges.ref: [60] Vasil Papakroni. Data carving: Identifying and removing irrelevancies in the data. Master's thesis, West Virginia University, 2013.
edges.evidence: PEEKING2 [60] is a far more aggressive "data pruner" than TEAK and combines data reduction operators, feature weighting, and Principal Component Analysis(PCA).

edges.ref: [69] Martin J. Shepperd and Steven G. MacDonell. Evaluating prediction systems in software project estimation. Information & Software Technology, 5...
edges.evidence: We assess performance via Standardized Error(SE) ... This measure is derived from Standardized Accuracy(SA) defined by Shepperd & MacDonnell [69] (SE = 1 - SA).

edges.ref: [56] Nikolaos Mittas and Lefteris Angelis. Ranking and clustering software cost estimation models through a multiple comparisons algorithm. IEEE TS...
edges.evidence: This study ranks methods using the Scott-Knott procedure recommended by Mittas & Angelis in their 2013 IEEE TSE paper [56].

edges.ref: [18] Bradley Efron and Robert J Tibshirani. An introduction to the bootstrap. Mono. Stat. Appl. Probab. Chapman and Hall, London, 1993.
edges.evidence: For a justification of the use of non-parametric bootstrapping, see Efron & Tibshirani [18, p220-223].

edges.target: A12 effect size (Vargha & Delaney, via Arcuri & Briand)
edges.ref: [1] A. Arcuri and L. Briand. A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering. In ICSE'11, pag...
edges.evidence: Vargha and Delaney's non-parametric A12 effect size test ... This test was recently endorsed by Arcuri and Briand at ICSE'11 [1].

edges.ref: [29] Vigdis By Kampenes, Tore Dybaa, Jo Erskine Hannay, and Dag I. K. Sjoberg. A systematic review of effect size in software engineering experimen...
edges.evidence: For a justification of the use of effect size tests see Shepperd & MacDonell [69]; Kampenes [29]; and Kocaguneli et al. [38].

edges.target: Effect-size warning (Kocaguneli et al., Distributed development)
edges.ref: [38] Ekrem Kocaguneli, Thomas Zimmermann, Christian Bird, Nachiappan Nagappan, and Tim Menzies. Distributed development considered harmful? In ICSE...
edges.evidence: These researchers warn that even if an hypothesis test declares two populations to be "significantly" different, then that result is misleading if the "effect size" is very small.

edges.ref: [64] D. Posnett, V. Filkov, and P. Devanbu. Ecological inference in empirical software engineering. In Proceedings of ASE'11, 2011.
edges.evidence: "Ecological inference" is the conceit that "what holds for all, also holds for parts of the population" [45, 64]. To avoid ecological inference, our rig in Figure 7 runs separately for each data set.

edges.target: Local vs global lessons (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [45] Tim Menzies, Andrew Butcher, David R. Cok, ... Thomas Zimmermann. Local versus global lessons for defect prediction and effort estimation. IEE...
edges.evidence: To avoid ecological inference, our rig in Figure 7 runs separately for each data set.

edges.target: Row+column reduction result (Chen, Boehm, Menzies, Port)
edges.ref: [10] Zhihao Chen, Barry Boehm, Tim Menzies, and Daniel Port. Finding the right data for software cost modeling. IEEE Software, 22:38-46, 2005.
edges.evidence: Their results are very clear: as the number of rows shrink, better estimates come from using fewer columns.

edges.target: Least-squares variance vs. number of columns (Miller)
edges.ref: [52] A. Miller. Subset Selection in Regression (second edition). Chapman & Hall, 2002.
edges.evidence: Miller [52] explains why this is so: the variance of a linear model learned by minimizing least-squares error decreases as the number of columns in the model decreases.

edges.target: Straw-man comparison guideline (Cohen, Empirical Methods for AI)
edges.ref: [13] P.R. Cohen. Empirical Methods for Artificial Intelligence. MIT Press, 1995.
edges.evidence: Cohen [13] strongly advises such "straw man" comparisons, since sometimes, they reveal that the supposedly superior method is actually overly complex.

edges.ref: [67] Mary Shaw. The coming-of-age of software architecture research. In ICSE '01, pages 656-, 2001.
edges.evidence: Mary Shaw [67] noted that it can take up to a decade for research innovations to become stable and then another decade after that to become widely popular.

edges.ref: [25] M. Jorgensen and M. Shepperd. A systematic review of software development cost estimation studies, January 2007.
edges.evidence: Jorgensen and Shepperd reported on hundreds of research papers dating back to the 1970s devoted to the topic, over half of which propose some innovation

edges.ref: [72] R. Valerdi. Convergence of expert opinion via the wideband delphi method: An application in cost estimation models. In Incose International Sy...
edges.evidence: he once recruited 40 experts to three expert sessions, each of which ran for three hours. Assuming a 7.5 hour day, then that study took 3*3*40/7.5 = 48 days.

edges.target: NASA use of COCOMO (Dabney IV&V ROI study)
edges.ref: [16] J. B. Dabney. Return on investment for IV&V, 2002-2004. NASA funded study.
edges.evidence: NASA routinely checks software estimates in COCOMO [16].

edges.target: Data mining techniques for SEE (Dejaeger et al.)
edges.ref: [17] Karel Dejaeger, Wouter Verbeke, David Martens, and Bart Baesens. Data mining techniques for software effort estimation: A comparative study. I...
edges.evidence: CART and Knear(n) still have currency: recent results from IEEE TSE 2008 and 2012 still endorse their use for effort estimation [17, 32, 35]

not_reuse_examples: [4,19,20,65,74,76] Black/Freiman/Herd/Putnam/Walston/Wolverton: historical narrative of how Boehm built SCEP/COCOMO in the 1970s; not used by this paper's experiments.
[63] Popper, [47] Menzies 'Problems with precision', [49,58] errata examples: philosophy-of-science motivation for reporting negative results only.
[26,23,24,62,57] Jorgensen/Passos/planning-poker: background on expert vs model estimation, nothing adopted or run.
[2,28,30-33,39-42] CBR literature list ('used extensively'), [9,14,15,36,37,44,51,55] meta-level techniques list: survey citations only.
notes: Empirical negative-result benchmark (Menzies/Boehm self-heavy): COCOMO-II vs LOC, CART, Knear, ATLM, TEAK, PEEKING2 on 4 COCOMO datasets; NASA10 and proprietary COC05 are new here (no prior ref), A12 has no direct Vargha&Delaney ref.
